l1: A stone blade secured to a wooden handle. More effective than either alone.

l1: A cord stretched low across a path, which sets off a trap when touched.
l2: A tripwire lets the animal spring the trap itself, so it can be set and left.
l3: Known mainly from ethnographic practice; the materials rarely survive.

l2: Dried fish keeps for months. A large seasonal run of fish becomes food for the whole year.
l3: Post-holes near shores, together with large numbers of fish bones, point to drying and storage.

l1: A channel dug to carry water away from a dwelling or field.
l2: Keeping water out of a floor or away from crops makes a place livable and farmable.
l3: Ditches appear in excavation as bands of different soil that filled them in.

l3: Firebrands leave no specific trace; their use is inferred from fire use generally.

l2: A thrown spear reaches an animal before it gets close, which makes hunting safer.
l3: Whether early wooden spears were thrown or thrust is judged from their balance and shape, and remains debated.

l1: A long, heavy spear used for thrusting.
l2: A long thrusting spear keeps a large animal at a distance while the hunter holds his ground.
l3: Preserved wooden spears and wear on stone points help separate thrusting from throwing weapons.

l1: Wood split or cut into beams and planks.
l2: Straight, even timber is what frames, boats and furniture are built from.
l3: Tool marks on preserved wood show how it was split and shaped.

l1: A place where stone is dug or broken out of the ground.
l2: Good stone is not everywhere. A quarry is a place people returned to again and again to get it.
l3: Quarries leave pits, waste flakes and abandoned blanks in large quantities.

l2: A fire is built up in stages; kindling bridges the gap between a spark and a log.
l3: Kindling burns away completely; its use is inferred from fire-making itself.

l1: A small shaped stick driven into the ground or into wood to hold things in place.
l2: Pegs hold down tents, snares and hides being stretched, and they join wood without nails.
l3: Pegs survive in waterlogged sites, and peg holes are visible in preserved woodwork.

l2: Sinkers hold a net upright in the water, so it catches fish instead of floating on the surface.
l3: Notched or grooved small stones found near water are often identified as sinkers.

l2: Striking sparks is a fast, portable way to make fire, with no need to carry an ember.
l3: Wear marks on some flint tools have been interpreted as evidence of striking sparks; the interpretation is debated.
caution: Named 'Flint Spark' until 2026-09. Gameplay entry. The recipe is a simplification, and the date and evidence for this entry have not yet been checked against a subject-level source.

l1: A blade set across a handle for loosening soil and pulling weeds.
l2: A hoe breaks up soil and clears weeds, one of the most basic tasks in tending plants.
l3: Stone and bone blades with soil polish are the evidence.

l1: A place set aside for making things.
l2: Separating work into areas — knapping here, butchering there — shows planning and organised activity.
l3: Clusters of debris from a single activity, such as knapping flakes, mark work areas at a site.
caution: Named 'Workshop' until 2026-09. Gameplay entry. The recipe is a simplification, and the date and evidence for this entry have not yet been checked against a subject-level source.

l1: Living plants for food, medicine, fiber, and tools.
l2: Plants are the foundation of human diet and material culture. Every ecosystem offers edible plants, medicinal plants, and plants for fiber or construction.
l3: Plant processing gave us fiber, food preservation, medicine, and poisons.

l1: Dried grass and reeds for thatching and bedding.
l2: Grass provides insulation, water resistance, and structure when dried and bundled together.
l3: Thatch made from grass and reeds is one of the oldest roofing materials.

l1: Woven or felted fibers forming a flexible material.
l2: Cloth can be made from plant fibers or animal hair by weaving or felting strands together.
l3: Early cloth provided protection from weather and later became a medium for decoration and social signaling.
ev: Fiber fragments, tool impressions, pictorial evidence

l1: Bundled grass or reeds tied together to form weatherproof covering.
l2: Thatch is a durable roofing material that sheds water and insulates. It can last 30+ years if properly maintained.
l3: Thatch roofs require specific construction knowledge and are particularly suited to areas with abundant grass or reeds.
ev: Archaeological remains of thatched structures across multiple continents

l1: Open mesh of knotted cordage for catching fish and small game.
l2: Nets dramatically increase hunting and fishing efficiency by creating a boundary that animals cannot see or understand. A single net can trap many animals where a spear might catch one.
l3: Nets appear in the archaeological record as impressions, wear patterns on tools, and in artistic representations. They are older than agriculture and remain one of humanity's most important food-acquisition technologies.
ev: Net fragments, artistic depictions, tool wear patterns

l1: Cordage twisted into thread, sharpened bone shaped into needle.
l2: Thread and needle enable sewn clothing, which allowed humans to adapt clothing to fit their body precisely, crucial for surviving cold climates.
l3: Sewn clothing appears in the archaeological record around 40,000 years ago, coinciding with human expansion into colder regions.
ev: Bone needles, tool marks, sewn fabric fragments

l1: Smoke created by burning bone and fiber to repel insects and animals.
l2: Smudge fires create dense smoke that repels biting insects and keeps animals at a distance. Critical for survival in warm climates with aggressive insect swarms.
l3: Smudging remains an important technique for both insect control and ceremonial purposes in many cultures.
ev: Ash deposits with bone char, ethnographic evidence

l1: Thatch made from bundled grass, reeds, or straw, used to cover and insulate roofs.
l2: Thatched roofs are remarkably durable, shedding water effectively while providing excellent insulation. A well-built thatch roof can last 30-60 years.
l3: Thatching is a specialized craft requiring knowledge of local materials and building techniques. Thatched structures remain common in regions with abundant grass or reed.
ev: Archaeological remains of thatched structures, reconstructions

l1: Thin cordage made from plant fibers, useful for fine work and delicate applications.
l2: Plant-derived fibers can be processed into extremely thin, strong threads suitable for sewing fine cloth, making nets with small mesh, and detailed basketry.
l3: Different plants yield fibers with different properties: flax produces strong fine thread, hemp produces rough strong cordage, and various plants yield specialty fibers.

l1: Thatch woven into flat, flexible sheets for flooring, walls, or portable shelter.
l2: Mats provide insulation and waterproofing. They can be rolled up for transport, making them ideal for nomadic peoples. Tightly woven mats can also serve as walls or temporary shelters.
l3: Mat-weaving remains an important technology in cultures with abundant reed or grass. Mat designs reflect regional plant availability and cultural preferences.
ev: Mat fragments, impressions in clay, artwork

l1: Long fibers extracted from flax plants, processed into strong, fine thread and linen cloth.
l2: Flax fibers are exceptionally strong and fine, producing the smoothest and strongest plant-derived fabric. Linen made from flax resists rotting and improves with age and washing.
l3: Flax production requires specialized knowledge: planting, retting (water-soaking), breaking, scutching (beating), and hackling (combing). Ancient Egyptians prized linen for both clothing and mummification wraps.
ev: Flax seeds, processed fiber, linen cloth fragments, artwork

l1: Wooden trap with net webbing that fish swim into but cannot escape from easily.
l2: Fish traps are passive fishing technology that allows continuous capture without constant attention. They can be left in place and checked periodically, making fishing more efficient.
l3: Different fish traps are optimized for different species and water conditions. Some rely on funnel entrances that fish can find but cannot navigate back through.
ev: Preserved traps, artistic depictions, tool wear patterns

l1: Net weighted with stones or bone, designed to sink and trap fish and aquatic animals.
l2: Weighted nets sink to the bottom and can cover a larger area. When deployed strategically in water, they trap fish trying to escape. The Retiarius (net-fighter) of ancient Rome used a similar concept as a weapon.
l3: Weighted casting nets remain a highly effective fishing technique. A skilled fisher can cast a weighted net and retrieve a catch with a single motion.
ev: Net weights (stones with grooves), net fragments, artwork

l1: Decorated cloth created by stitching thread into existing cloth to form patterns and images.
l2: Embroidery adds aesthetic value and symbolic meaning to cloth. It transforms plain fabric into art, and in many cultures, embroidery patterns communicate identity, status, and cultural affiliation.
l3: Different cultures developed distinct embroidery styles. Chinese silk embroidery, Middle Eastern gold thread work, and European needlepoint each represent sophisticated artistic traditions.

l1: Cloth dyed or decorated to blend with natural surroundings for hunting or military purposes.
l2: Camouflage works by breaking up the visual outline and matching the colors of the environment. Effective camouflage requires understanding local colors, textures, and lighting conditions.
l3: Modern military camouflage patterns evolved from hunting traditions. Each environment requires different patterns: forest, desert, snow, and urban camouflage all use different color and shape combinations.
ev: Historical hunting garments, military uniforms, natural dye analysis

l1: Plant fibers broken down into a mushy consistency for papermaking or insulation.
l2: Pulp is created by soaking plant fibers in water and beating them until they break down into fine fibers. This pulp can be spread thin and dried to make paper, or used for insulation and padding.
l3: Chinese papermaking, developed around 2,000 years ago, refined pulp-making techniques. Quality paper requires controlling fiber length, fiber distribution, and the density of the final sheet.
ev: Paper fragments, papermaking equipment, historical documents
